title: Spiritual Offspring and the Divine Vineyard
english: Salvation. An ancient wise man commanded that horsemen be distinguished from mere riders, calling one false and the other praiseworthy; for he who holds back without skill, not guiding the horse with reins, is merely a rider, as the aforementioned wise man demonstrated, whereas the one practicing the art of horsemanship is called righteous. Immediately, as the great prophet Elijah was being taken up, Elisha the God-inspired one cried out, 'Father, father, the chariot of Israel and its horsemen!' (2 Kings 2:12). For the one riding most excellently, having guided his own vehicle, ought to be called a horseman, not merely a rider.

Since this distinction between horseman and rider exists, it is not the horsemen but the passengers who will be disgraced, as they slumber while those riding with skill are sober and watchful, guiding the reins; therefore, those proven as victors bring victory, while the passengers of false horses are disgraced. Those of Judah are being disgraced, but the house of Joseph lives and shall be saved by the King of Kings, God; from the parallel of Joseph and Judah, the Savior who became man exists, since from Judah he rose up and provided food to those suffering from famine and starvation, so that he might ultimately be shown to be full of bread, having received the greatest prosperity; for it is said concerning the offspring of Mary that those who previously famished because they lacked spiritual food were filled with good things, which their intelligent Joseph provided. Indeed, he has come to such abundance that, just as in the wilderness he nourished those deprived of food into a flock, he fed large multitudes from very few loaves.

Having strengthened the house of Judah and the house of Joseph, God promises to let them dwell, for no other reason than that he loved them. But when will this be? When they are enjoying what they have; he persuaded them with promises, concerning which it is written here: 'Eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it come upon the heart, what God has prepared for those who love him' (1 Cor 2:9). And the promised things shall be for them, in the manner of 'I have not turned them away, but I look upon and care for them,' the Lord being 'their God.' For I will hear of them being exceedingly fruitful according to Ephraim (Hosea 2:14), interpreting fruitfulness as their intellect having eaten and rejoiced, as in wine...

Having been harvested from the true vine, about which much clarity has already been given. What results from the drinking of the divine wine? Or is it to be made glad from beholding the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven and other things which possess a high contemplation, by which one will see God, having approached with a pure heart 'by the character of his subsistence,' as he calls the existing one an 'image' and character 'of the invisible God': 'He who has seen me has seen the Father' (John 14:9)?

Not only will these themselves enjoy the promises of the holy visions, but also the children themselves whom they have begotten by divine instruction and imitation of an excellent life. For the Apostle in Christ writes to the Corinthians and the Galatians: to the former, 'Through the gospel I have begotten you' (2 Cor 5:17); to the latter, 'My children, whom I again labor for until Christ is formed in you' (Gal 4:19). And Peter, the foremost of the apostles, writes as to his own children the letter he has engraved: 'As children of obedience, not being conformed to the former manner of life' (1 Pet 1:14). And Barnabas also, an apostle with Paul, having been placed at the circumcision, having sent a letter to the faithful according to the gospel, addresses it as to sons and daughters. And the hymnist addresses those being born from him according to virtue: 'Come, children, listen to me, I will teach you the fear of the Lord. Who is the man who desires life and loves to see good days?' (Ps 33:8).

The children will be made glad in mind, in the heart so named, in no one other than their Lord God, saying to each of those living according to the divine Gospel: 'Enter into the joy of your Lord' (Matt 25:21). 'I will signal them and I will bring them in, because I will redeem them, and they shall be multiplied because they were many; and I will sow them among the peoples, and those far off shall remember me. They shall bring up their children and return. And I will bring them back from the land of Egypt and from the Assyrians, and I will bring them in, and into Galilee and into Lebanon I will bring them, and not even one of them shall be left' (Zech 10:8-10). The Lord, intending to bring in those alienated by the manner of captivity, does not do this all at once, but by signaling His benevolence to those receiving it. This—

title: Spiritual Multiplication and the Seed of Abraham
english: The practice of contemplation is especially brought forward in the Gospels; for Jesus, desiring to give rest to souls, says, 'Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and you will find rest for your souls; and take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart; for my yoke is good and my burden is light' (Matt 11:28-30). By saying, 'Come to me and I will give you rest,' he signifies how he judges them worthy to receive him into himself so that they might lift off his yoke, which is good, and the light burden.

This divine exhortation is also brought forward in Isaiah, with the Holy Spirit crying out: 'Shine, shine, Jerusalem, for your light has come, and the glory of your God has risen upon you. Behold, darkness and gloom will cover the earth, but upon you the Lord will appear' (Isa 60:1-2). He emphasized as a sign that it is fitting to be enlightened by the existing true light: 'But upon you the Lord will appear, and the glory of your God will be seen,' signifying how the royal souls, held by the King of all, go forth by the light of the one receiving them, and the called nations into the gospel by the brightness of the glorious Church, as Jerusalem is being led upward, since one sees 'the peace of God surpassing all understanding' (Phil 4:7) through perfect height and royal eminence.

For whose sake does he signify and receive them, saying in harmony: 'Because I will redeem them and multiply them, because they were many' (Hos 2:23)? He redeems them from the law of captivity of shoulders and unclad tyrants who had led them away from their own commonwealth.

The manner and how the restoration to liberty is exalted lies in other writings. Indeed, one of the saints cried out to the benefactor: 'My joy, redeem me from those who persecute me'; and again: 'Redeem me, Lord God of truth.' Peter, the foremost of Christ's disciples, makes manifest a turning away of those who had rushed from their former wickedness, writing to the faithful: 'You were not redeemed from your futile, ancestral way of life with corruptible gold or silver, but in the precious blood of Christ, the lamb without blemish and without spot' (1 Pet 1:18-19). The Savior, having redeemed, promised this.

The statement, 'I will multiply them because they were many,' is necessarily relevant; it refers not only to a multiplication in number, but also to an excellence in honor, similar to the blessing spoken by God toward Abraham: 'I will increase him, and I will multiply him, and I will bless him, and he shall be a blessing; a father of many nations, being revealed as a gift of God.' He becomes a father of many nations not merely according to the flesh, but according to the intelligible, clearly meaning that his children and sons are those who do his works and possess faith.

Indeed, the Savior himself, most strongly rebuking those who claim to have Abraham as a father according to the flesh, said: 'If you are children of Abraham, do the works of Abraham' (John 15:16). By this understanding, 'the vessel of election,' the apostle Paul writes to the Church, clarifying how the holy patriarch is a father of the nations, asserting: 'As many as are of faith, these are sons of Abraham, being blessed with him' (Galatians 3:7). The same view is proposed by that prophecy brought forth in Isaiah: 'The few shall become thousands, and the least a great nation' (Isaiah 60:22).

Taking these things in a sensory way provokes laughter, since many saints did not bear children at all: namely Elijah and Elisha, and John the Baptist, of whom no one greater was praised in deed or holy knowledge; they in no way bore children, so it is appropriate to understand the multiplication of those possessing such promises spiritually, 'because they were many.' For the righteous did not begin to multiply and become many only in this present life, according to the assigned understanding; for they were many even before this present life.

These, being many, were like seeds that he sowed among the peoples so that they might partake of their virtue. Just as seeds thrown into the earth transform the lying soil to become offspring and fruit, so those sown among the peoples and the nations bring those whom they have sown into their own quality, as if becoming imitators of their virtue. No one errs in saying that those who heard were sown by Jesus, saying: 'Go and make disciples of all nations' (Matthew 28:19); and even to the same in the [Gospel] according to John: 'For this reason I said to you,' that is, I appointed and demonstrated, 'that you might go and bear more fruit' (John 15:16), and the fruit...

title: The Migration of the Soul
english: He will be glorified.

I think that in this way the saints are taken captive with the peoples and into Babylon and Assyria, so that by imparting their own virtue they might show themselves to be ears of grain and offspring of saving seeds. This will be consistent with the remembering of the Lord by those who had drifted away from him through sins and impiety. Especially these promises fit those who have believed from the nations. For it has been said concerning them in the 121st and 1st Psalm: 'All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord, and all the families of the nations shall worship before him, for the kingdom is the Lord's and he is the ruler of the nations.' For how could he not rule and be the master of those remembered who have turned to him, as to worship and glorify the one who holds them as a benefactor?

What will follow for those remembering the All-King, or that it might happen in a non-literal sense regarding 'the city of the living God,' being heavenly, according to what was said: 'You who are far off, remember the Lord, and let Jerusalem ascend to your heart.' Those having been benefited by their own Savior, being as it were servants and many-children by spiritual upbringing, will rear their own children, imparting intellectual food, as it is announced concerning each one according to the writing of the divine Proverbs: 'A righteous father brings up his children well.'

This can be understood toward spiritual upbringing, and also according to history; for being a righteous father, Zechariah reared well John the Baptist, who was his child, just as Abraham reared Isaac, and Isaac reared Jacob; and he himself, Paul the divine, reared profitably and praiseworthily those whom he had begotten through the gospel. For it is possible to hear him writing to the Corinthians: 'I gave you milk.' Similarly Peter writes to the faithful in the dispersion: 'Having been born again, not of corruptible seed, but of incorruptible through the word of the living and abiding God, as newborn babes, long for the spiritual milk, so that in it you may grow unto salvation.' In this same way also the evangelist John, having begotten the disciples through him by a way of instruction, writes to the whole Church: 'Children, keep yourselves from idols.' Toward the rearing...

They will find their own children, those who have become fathers, and they will turn them back with divine exhortations and instructions, so that they may no longer be with evildoers in ungodly lands, this being granted by God, as He Himself said: 'I will bring them back from Egypt, and from the Assyrians I will receive them' (Exodus 20:22; Jeremiah 31:8), so that they may no longer be subdued by the spiritual tyrant of Egypt, nor be held by the ruler of the Assyrians, called 'the great mind' because of the cunning and absurdity of thoughts, which the common people do not refute, but only those speaking God-wisely say: 'For we do not ignore his thoughts.'

It is possible to call the same tyrant the ruler of the Egyptians and the Assyrians through another energy; and even if different evil powers were signified by various names, it does not grieve, for such a thing is not impossible, with many being 'rulers and powers of this darkness, but also cosmic rulers and spiritual wickedness' (Ephesians 6:12).

The provider of great gifts, having freed from Egypt and Assyria those who are well-rearing their children and those who begot them, promises to bring them into Gilead and Lebanon, with no evil king still bothering them. And see if he brings into Gilead those who strive to have the migration of martyrdom, the movement from wickedness into virtue; for the one repenting from sin into righteousness, from ungodliness into godliness, is being migrated, as the righteous are being migrated in a different way from the introduction of instruction into the following progress, and from that into the succeeding one, until that very end, with which nothing other good exists, being the final object of desire.

In this way, concerning those being migrated, the hymnist says: 'They shall go from strength to strength' (Psalm 84:7). And they are also migrated from the shadow of the law into its truth, those having ascended above the killing letter (2 Corinthians 3:6) and becoming in the life-giving Spirit. It must be supervised whether even a partial knowing and prophesying undergoes migration; but the witness of the migration or sojourning shall be, acting contrary to itself, possessing the proof. Those brought in by God into Gilead are being brought into Lebanon.
